title: Re-using a text for a new purpose

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Re-use a source text’s content in a different form and style in your own words; write in the manner of a given text.

blocks.heading: The directed response
blocks.text: A directed response is a new text written from a source for a form, audience and purpose the task sets, re-using the source’s content in a new style. It is not a summary of the source, and it is not a copy of its wording: the task sets a new form for a new reader, and the content arrives in the clothing the task asks for. Paper 1’s Section A sets it at 150–200 words from an unseen text of about 550–750, and the task carries ten marks — five for the reading of the source, five for the writing.

blocks.heading: Reshaping the source
blocks.text: Reshaping a source runs in two steps. First select: from everything the source contains, keep the content the new purpose needs — the facts a diary writer would know, the viewpoint a reply must answer — and leave the rest. Then change: the register, the voice and the structure go over to the new form, and the content arrives in your own words. A report of a flood for the safety officer keeps dates and figures and sheds the memoir’s images; the same flood as a note to a neighbour keeps the warmth and sheds the sections.

blocks.heading: Re-use and lifting
blocks.text: Re-using content means keeping what the source says — its facts, its viewpoint, its people — while putting it into your own words. Lifting phrases or sentences from the source is copying, not re-use: a response that carries the source’s sentences into the new form has changed its clothing without changing its voice, which is the one thing reshaping must do. The test is the sentence: could the source’s writer have written it? If yes, it is theirs, not yours.

blocks.heading: Worked example: one source, two responses
blocks.text: A source tells of a school that turned unused land into an urban farm: yields, a teacher’s quote, the launch day, the mayor’s promise of funding. As a speech to the school assembly, the response selects the pupils’ achievement and the teacher’s pride, addresses the hall directly ("Good morning — you did this"), and saves the mayor’s promise for a close that asks for applause. As a report to the education office, the same content arrives in sections — background, outcomes, recommendation — with the yield figures first and the mayor’s promise as "funding pledged". Two forms, one source: selection and register did the whole work.

blocks.heading: In the exam
blocks.text: The directed response is the first task of Paper 1, and it sets the pattern for the whole paper: read the unseen text of about 550–750 words accurately, then write to a brief. Ten marks, five for the reading and five for the writing, and the two are inseparable — the reading marks are for drawing on the source’s content perceptively, which a lifted or summarised response does not do. Practise the two steps until they are one: select for the new purpose, then write every sentence for the new reader.

blocks.heading: Two ways to lose the source
blocks.text: The first error is lifting: phrases and sentences copied from the source into the response, which is copying rather than re-use and fails the writing half of the task at the level of the sentence. The second is summarising: the source retold in its own order, which produces a shorter source rather than a new text. Both have the same cure: select for the new purpose, then write every sentence afresh for the new reader. A third error shadows both — adding material the source does not support — and the rule is that every fact in a directed response traces back to the source.
